extracted.intended_audience: trial judges, juries, and patent litigators in U.S. patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions and legal standards for evaluating patent invalidity and related defenses (e.g., anticipation, on‑sale bar, obviousness, enablement, written description, inequitable conduct) in U.S. federal court trials. Provides elements, definitions, and factors jurors should apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to Practice / Ready for Patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is reduced to practice when it has been (1) constructed or performed within the scope of the patent claims; and (2) determined that it works for its intended purpose. The claimed invention is ready for patenting when there is reason to believe it would work for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly (e.g., in on‑sale bar and conception analyses). Ready for patenting can be shown either by reduction to practice or by drawings/descriptions sufficient to allow a person of ordinary skill in the art to make or use the invention. Citations: 35 U.S.C. §102(a),(b) and multiple Federal Circuit cases (e.g., Cooper v. Goldfarb).

rubrics_metrics.name: On‑Sale Bar (35 U.S.C. §102(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if more than one year before the filing date an embodiment of the claimed invention was both (1) subject to a commercial offer for sale in the United States; and (2) ready for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Definition of commercial 'offer for sale': made if another party could make a binding contract by simply accepting the offer; embodiment must have been actually sold or offered for sale (no actual sale required). Essential question is whether there was an attempt to obtain commercial benefit. The invention must have been conceived before any offer can exist. Ready for patenting is defined by reduction to practice or sufficient drawings/descriptions. See Pfaff v. Wells Electronics and cited authorities. If a factual issue on date of invention exists, jury instructions on determining invention date should be given.

Examples/Notes: the instruction emphasizes conception and readiness; citations include Pfaff, August Tech, and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is conceived when the inventor(s) forms in his mind a definite and permanent idea of the complete and operative invention, as it will be used in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception is a prerequisite to an offer for sale and is relevant to priority disputes. If date of invention is in dispute, the jury should be instructed how to determine it. Case cites: Bd. of Educ. ex rel. Fla. State Univ. v. Am. Bioscience, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental Use Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain activities are experimental if they are a legitimate effort to test claimed features of the invention or to determine if the invention will work for its intended purpose. So long as the primary purpose is experimentation, it does not matter that the public used the invention or that the inventor incidentally derived profit from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only experimentation by or under the control of the inventor (or assignee) qualifies. Experimentation must relate to claimed features and be for technological improvement rather than commercial exploitation. Commercial exploitation must be merely incidental to experimentation. A test done primarily for marketing is not experimental. If defendant shows it is highly probable there was a prior public use or sale, burden shifts to plaintiff to show experimental purpose. Citations: Clock Spring, Lisle Corp., Allen Eng’g, and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed Publication (anticipation / prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the invention was described in a printed publication either before it was invented or more than one year prior to the U.S. filing date. A printed publication must have been maintained in some tangible form (e.g., printed pages, microfilm, internet publication) and sufficiently accessible to persons interested in the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility: 'publicly accessible' means distributed or made available so that persons interested and ordinarily skilled exercising reasonable diligence can locate it; not necessary to be available to every member of the public. An issued patent or published patent application is a printed publication. The printed publication's disclosure must be enabling — complete enough to enable one of ordinary skill to use the invention without undue experimentation; jurors should consider what would have been within the knowledge of a person of ordinary skill at the relevant time. Citations: 35 U.S.C. §102(a),(b) and numerous cases (In re NTP, Orion IP v. Hyundai, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Invention by Another (35 U.S.C. §102(a),(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the invention was invented by another person in the United States before it was invented by the patentee (and that prior inventor did not abandon, suppress, or conceal the invention). The defendant must show it is highly probable that before the patentee, the third party reduced to practice a product or method that included all claim elements, or that the third party first conceived and exercised reasonable diligence to reduce to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prior device must have been sufficiently developed that one skilled in the art would recognize it would work for its intended purpose. If the prior invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed, it does not anticipate; abandonment/suppression requires active concealment or unreasonable delay in making the invention public. It is not necessary that the patentee had knowledge of the prior invention. Case citations provided (Teva v. AstraZeneca, Monsanto v. Mycogen, etc.). Note: further instructions required where priority is submitted to the jury (conception dates and reduction to practice comparisons, diligence issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Patent (anticipation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the invention was patented in the United States or a foreign country before it was invented by the patentee or more than one year before the patentee filed a U.S. application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If date of invention is disputed, the jury should be instructed on determining that date. Cited authorities include 35 U.S.C. §102(a)-(b) and cases such as Adv. Display Sys. v. Kent State Univ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior U.S. Application / Published U.S. Patent Application (35 U.S.C. §§102(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was described in a published U.S. patent application or U.S. patent filed by another person before the invention was made by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If invention date is a factual issue, instruct jury on how to determine it. Citations: 35 U.S.C. §§102(e)(1)-(2); In re Giacomini, Sun Studs, In re Wertheim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — General Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is invalid as 'obvious' if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made. Unlike anticipation, obviousness may be shown by considering more than one prior art item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors must avoid hindsight and not use the patent as a road map to select/combine prior art. Put oneself in the place of a POSITA at the time of invention. The defendant must prove obviousness is highly probable. Sources: KSR v. Teleflex, Graham v. John Deere, and other Federal Circuit precedent. The instruction then directs evaluation of four specific factors (below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — Factor 1: Scope and Content of the Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what prior art may be considered; prior art includes items received into evidence and any references that disclose information designed to solve problems or needs addressed by the patent or that have obvious uses beyond their main purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties stipulate the prior art, list it; if disputed, jurors must determine which references are reasonably relevant to solving problems addressed by the patent. Add instructions on on‑sale/publication bars as appropriate. Citations: KSR, Ruiz, Wang Labs., In re Clay, In re Wood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — Factor 2: Differences Between the Claimed Invention and the Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze relevant differences between the prior art and the claimed invention from the viewpoint of a POSITA at the time of invention; determine the impact of those differences on obviousness of the invention as a whole, not merely a portion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require precise teaching in the prior art; consider inferences and creative steps a POSITA would have employed. If combination of known elements yielded predictable results, that supports obviousness; unexpected results or 'teaching away' support nonobviousness. A claim is not proved obvious merely by showing each element was independently known; consider whether a reason existed at the time to combine elements (from prior art, background knowledge, market demand, or common sense). Conduct separate analysis for each claim. Citations: KSR, Abbott Labs., Graham, Stratoflex, Medtronic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — Factor 3: Level of Ordinary Skill in the Art
rubrics_metrics.description: The obviousness determination is from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; that person is presumed to know all prior art determined reasonably relevant and is a person of ordinary creativity who can use common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties agree to a level of skill, include it. If not, consider evidence including (1) level of education and experience of persons in the field at time of invention (including inventor), (2) types of problems encountered in the art at the time, and (3) sophistication of the technology including rate of innovation. Citations: KSR, Graham, Ruiz, Envtl Designs v. Union Oil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — Factor 4: Secondary Considerations (Indicators of Nonobviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that, if established, may indicate that the invention would not have been obvious. No single factor is dispositive; consider the invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only appropriate instructions. Examples of secondary considerations listed: (1) commercial success due to merits of claimed invention rather than promotion; (2) long‑felt need satisfied by invention; (3) others tried and failed to solve the problem; (4) others copied the claimed invention; (5) unexpected superior results over closest prior art; (6) praise or surprise expressed by others in the field or defendant; (7) acceptance of licenses due to merits. These are relevant only if there is a nexus between the factor and the claimed invention. Citations: Graham, United States v. Adams, Perkin‑Elmer, WL Gore, Stratoflex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement Requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent must disclose sufficient information to enable persons of ordinary skill in the field, at the time the priority application was filed, to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation. If not enabled, the claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents are written for POSITA and need not state information the POSITA would know. Some experimentation may be permissible; jurors may consider Wands factors in determining undue experimentation: (1) quantity of experimentation necessary; (2) amount of direction/guidance in the patent; (3) presence/absence of working examples; (4) nature of the invention; (5) state of the prior art; (6) relative skill of those in the art; (7) predictability of the art; (8) breadth of the claims. Burden: defendant must show lack of enablement is highly probable. Citations: 35 U.S.C. §112; Wands and many Federal Circuit cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent must contain a written description of the product or process claimed. The requirement ensures the applicant actually invented the claimed subject matter; the specification must describe each and every limitation of a claim in sufficient detail (exact claim words not required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfied if POSITA would recognize from the specification that the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter as of the filing date, even if claims changed later. Not necessary to spell out every detail or provide specific examples; enough must be included to convince POSITA the inventor possessed the full scope. Factors to consider: (i) nature and scope of claims, (ii) complexity/predictability/maturity of technology, (iii) existing knowledge in the field, (iv) scope and content of prior art. Burden: defendant must prove lack of written description by the highly probable standard. Citations: 35 U.S.C. §112; Ariad en banc and numerous cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unenforceability / Inequitable Conduct — General
rubrics_metrics.description: Inequitable conduct occurs when individuals substantively involved in prosecution of the patent engaged in affirmative acts of egregious misconduct or withheld/misrepresented/submitted false information material to examination, and acted with specific intent to deceive or mislead the PTO. Applicants owe a duty of candor, good faith, and honesty during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inequitable conduct is an equitable issue for the trial court (advisory jury may be used). Different burdens apply: inequitable conduct requires proof by the highly probable standard; the separate issue whether the PTO would have issued the patent 'but for' the omission uses the preponderance standard (as required by Therasense). The instruction suggests careful consideration before using an advisory jury because of complexity. Citations: Therasense, Avid, eSpeed, Dig. Control, Purdue, Bristol‑Myers Squibb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality in Inequitable Conduct (non‑disclosure cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is material if 'but for' the individual's failure to disclose or misrepresentation, the Patent and Trademark Office would not have allowed one or more claims of the patent. In other words, it is more likely than not that the PTO would not have allowed one or more claims if it had been aware of the withheld/true information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To decide whether the PTO would not have allowed a claim, use the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim(s) under consideration and apply the 'more likely than not' standard (how the PTO would have evaluated it). This is the materiality prong of inequitable conduct in non‑disclosure cases. (Further instructions continue beyond the excerpt.) Citations: Therasense and related precedent.
